costGuide.title: Mercedes M273 Engine Replacement Cost (UK)
costGuide.labourLine: Fitting a Mercedes M273 typically takes 14-18 hours at £65/hr (independent specialist rate) - confirm exact labour when comparing quotes, as V8 access in the engine bay is significantly tighter than the M272 V6.
paragraphs: The final cost of a Mercedes M273 engine replacement is heavily influenced by the V8's "valley pan" design, which houses the oil cooler and various seals that are prone to hardening and leaking over time. Replacement specialists will often recommend or include a valley pan seal inspection and refresh during the swap, which can add £400-£800 to the labour bill but prevents immediate post-swap oil leaks. See our full reconditioned engine cost guide for a detailed breakdown of what is included at each price tier.

failures.title: Mercedes M273 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Timing Chain Tensioner Failure (Early 2006-2008 Models)
items.whatHappens: The M273 introduced a revised timing chain tensioner design compared to the M113. On early production units (roughly 2006-2008), the tensioner's ratchet teeth can wear prematurely, allowing the timing chain to slacken and jump teeth. This causes a distinct metallic rattling noise on cold starts and, if ignored, leads to catastrophic valve-to-piston contact.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, replacing the tensioners and chains is viable, but it is a highly labour-intensive job requiring significant front-end strip-down or engine removal. If internal damage has already occurred, a full Mercedes M273 engine replacement is the only reliable solution.

items.title: Balance Shaft Sprocket Wear and Valley Pan Oil Leaks
items.whatHappens: Sharing architecture with the M272 V6, the M273 is susceptible to balance shaft sprocket wear, which can trigger camshaft correlation faults and check engine lights. Additionally, the V8's "valley pan" design houses the oil cooler and various seals that are prone to hardening and leaking over time, leading to oil loss and a persistent burning oil smell in the cabin.
items.repairVsReplace: Valley pan and oil cooler seal replacement is a standard, albeit labour-intensive, preventative repair. Balance shaft sprocket wear, if severe, may necessitate a reconditioned engine swap to avoid timing chain failure.

variants.title: M273 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: The M273 family covers several raw sub-codes that share the same core 90-degree V8 architecture but differ by displacement, intake manifold design, and calibration. Identifying your exact sub-code is critical, as components like the intake manifold, ECU, and engine mounts are not universally interchangeable. - Fitted to: Mercedes S-Class (W221 S 450), early Mercedes GL (X164 GL 450) - Key technical difference: The smallest displacement variant in the family (4498cc), featuring a specific intake manifold and lower-output calibration. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family timing chain tensioner and balance shaft wear pattern. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with 5.5L variants; the ECU, wiring loom, and exhaust systems differ significantly. - Fitted to: Mercedes S-Class (W221 S 450), CL (C216) (CL 450), Mercedes GL (X164 GL 450) - Key technical difference: The mid-range 4.7-litre variant (4663cc), widely used as the standard V8 option before the 5.5L took over in higher trims. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family timing chain and balance shaft patterns; intake manifold runner flaps can also stick, causing rough idle. - Interchange note: Physically similar to the 5.5L variants but requires the correct ECU calibration and specific exhaust routing to run safely. - Fitted to: Mercedes S-Class (W221 S 550), Mercedes E-Class (W211/W212 E 550), Mercedes ML (W164 ML 550), Mercedes GL (X164 GL 550) - Key technical difference: The high-output 5.5-litre variant (5461cc), featuring revised intake geometry and higher torque output, often paired with updated 7G-TRONIC transmissions. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family timing chain pattern, though later production years saw minor metallurgy improvements to the tensioners. - Interchange note: Cannot be swapped with 4.5L/4.7L units without extensive ECU and wiring modifications due to updated sensor layouts and fuel delivery requirements. - Fitted to: SL (R230) (SL 550), R-Class (W251) (R 550) - Key technical difference: The 5.5-litre variant tuned specifically for the SL roadster and R-Class MPV, featuring different accessory brackets, mounting points, and cooling system routing. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family timing chain and valley pan leak patterns.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement Mercedes M273 - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used Mercedes M273 is only advisable for lower-mileage host vehicles and *only* if accompanied by documented, stamped proof that the timing chain tensioners and balance shaft sprockets have been replaced with updated components. Without this history, the risk of inheriting the same catastrophic chain-jump issues is unacceptably high.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: This is the most recommended route for the M273. A proper reconditioned unit will include brand-new, updated timing chain tensioners, refreshed balance shaft sprockets, and a new valley pan seal kit, directly addressing the engine's known weak points out of the box.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified if your original M273 suffered a jumped timing chain that damaged the cylinder head, valves, or pistons. A specialist rebuild will machine the block, fit updated timing components, and ensure all oil galleries are clear of debris from the failed chain.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing a replacement is only half the job. Our network provides full supply and fit services, ensuring the engine is installed by Mercedes-specialist technicians with a nationwide warranty backing both the labour and the unit.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: For premium hosts like the W221 S-Class or W164 ML/GL, current UK market values typically sit between £5,000 and £18,000 . With a reconditioned M273 replacement costing from £3,800 (plus fitting), the repair cost generally represents 20-40% of the vehicle's value, making replacement financially viable. However, on sub-£5,000 early examples, we strongly advise evaluating the car's scrap or part-exchange value before committing to a full engine replacement.

items.question: What is the most common failure with the Mercedes M273 engine?
items.answer: The most documented failure pattern for the M273 is early timing chain tensioner wear and balance shaft sprocket degradation, typically occurring between 50,000 and 90,000 miles. Early warning signs include a distinct metallic rattling noise on cold starts and check engine lights for camshaft correlation faults, which can lead to catastrophic valve-to-piston contact if ignored.

items.question: Which Mercedes models use the M273 engine?
items.answer: The M273 is fitted to Mercedes-Benz premium models from 2006 to 2011, including the S-Class (W221), E-Class (W211/W212), ML/GL (W164/X164), and CL/SL (C216/R230). It powers badges ranging from the S 450 and E 550 to the ML 550 and GL 550, and you should always verify your exact sub-code via registration lookup before ordering parts.

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned Mercedes M273 engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned Mercedes M273 is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the well-documented timing chain tensioner and balance shaft sprocket failure risks. Used units carry a high probability of inheriting the same latent wear unless accompanied by stamped proof of a full chain and sprocket kit replacement, whereas a proper reconditioned M273 includes new, updated timing components and refreshed valley pan seals as standard.

items.question: What is the difference between the M273.920, M273.940, M273.950, and M273.960?
items.answer: The M273.920 is a 4.5L variant, the M273.940 is a 4.7L variant, and the M273.950/M273.960 are 5.5L variants. They all share the same core 90-degree V8 architecture and the same timing chain vulnerability, but they differ in displacement, intake manifold design, and ECU calibration, meaning they are not direct interchange replacements without extensive modifications.
